name: Pueblo of Jemez: the confirmed Spanish grant (Royce 662) and the taking of Jemez aboriginal land outside it (ICC Docket 137)
aka: Pueblo de Zia, Pueblo de Jemez and Pueblo de Santa Ana v. United States, ICC Docket 137
citation: Act of Congress confirming the Pueblo grants, 11 Stat. 374 (confirmed December 22, 1858; patented 1864), as listed by Royce; not a treaty
promises: Not a treaty. Royce lists the Jemez Pueblo grant as a Spanish grant of 1689, confirmed by the United States on December 22, 1858 (11 Stat. 374) and patented in 1864, of 17,510.45 acres. This was land the Pueblo kept.
Outside the grant, the Court of Claims held in 1964 that Jemez, Zia and Santa Ana together held Indian title in 1848 to 298,634 acres of the tract they claimed.

breaches.what: In the joint claim of Zia, Jemez and Santa Ana, the Commission found that the United States took 282,415.73 acres of the Pueblos' aboriginal land, worth $938,000 on the dates of taking, without paying compensation. It had earlier dated the takings to the 1905 Jemez Forest Reserve, settlers' entries and the 1936 grazing district.

breaches.what: The joint claim ended in a final judgment of $749,083.75 for the three Pueblos on a stipulation of settlement. A settlement is not a further finding.

landTaken: 282,415.73 acres held jointly with Zia and Santa Ana (Docket 137, 1970). The Commission held that a tract set apart for Jemez by Executive Order of December 19, 1906 and 908.48 acres set apart by Executive Order of October 4, 1915 were never taken.
compensation: Joint settlement of $749,083.75 for Zia, Jemez and Santa Ana (January 10, 1974), after a vacated 1971 award of $766,936.08.
today: Separately, Jemez sued under the Quiet Title Act for the Valles Caldera National Preserve. In 2023 the Tenth Circuit affirmed that Jemez had not shown aboriginal title to the whole Caldera but held, on the trial court's own findings, that Jemez still holds aboriginal title to Banco Bonito, and remanded for judgment on that point.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. The United States confirmed Jemez's Spanish grant of 17,510.45 acres in 1858. Outside it, Jemez, Zia and Santa Ana together held Indian title to 298,634 acres, a court held in 1964.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found the United States took 282,415.73 acres of that shared land without payment, through a 1905 forest reserve, settlers' entries and a 1936 grazing district.
plain.today: The joint claim was settled in 1974 for $749,083.75. In 2023 a federal appeals court held Jemez still holds aboriginal title to Banco Bonito in the Valles Caldera.
